title: A Note for New Muslims
summary: This app's own perspective, and practical guidance on navigating Sunni-Shia differences respectfully as you build your own practice.

body.text: Where this app is coming from

This app draws primarily from Sunni sources — the four madhhabs, and the Bukhari and Muslim hadith collections, already referenced throughout — since that reflects the majority global tradition and the background this content was written from. That's a starting point, not a verdict on Shia Islam's place within the wider faith; the previous three lessons aimed to describe both fairly rather than argue for one.

As a new Muslim, you'll likely meet, be befriended by, be guided by, or even marry into families from either tradition. Approaching a difference in tradition with curiosity rather than suspicion follows naturally from the shared ground the first lesson in this section covered — the overlap is much larger than the disagreement.
If you're not sure which you are (yet)

It's completely fine not to have settled views on contested historical or theological questions this early — or ever. Most Muslims worldwide are born into a tradition rather than choosing one through careful comparative study. If this specific question genuinely matters to you personally, learning directly from knowledgeable teachers within each tradition — not just a summary from an app — is the right next step, the same guidance already given elsewhere in this app for other contested details.

body.question: Is it disrespectful to ask a Muslim friend which one they are?
body.answer: Not inherently — tone and context matter, the same as asking about any personal or family background. A simple, genuinely curious question is normally welcomed; framing it as "which one is correct" can read as adversarial. The difference is usually in how you ask, not whether.

body.question: After these four lessons, what's one thing you'd want a Muslim friend from the other tradition to know you understand about their perspective?
